learning_objectives: Explain the importance of biology and its applications in Ethiopia.
Identify selected Ethiopian biologists and research institutions.
Identify the main parts of a compound light microscope and use magnification calculations.

sections.title: Biology and Its Applications
sections.content: Biology is the scientific study of living organisms and their interactions with the environment. It contributes to agriculture, medicine, public health, conservation, biotechnology, and food production. Biological knowledge can help communities prevent disease, improve crops and livestock, and protect biodiversity.

sections.title: Ethiopian Biologists and Research Institutions
sections.content: Examples of Ethiopian scientists include Dr Aklilu Lemma, known for research on endod (Phytolacca dodecandra) and its potential use in controlling freshwater snails involved in schistosomiasis transmission; Professor Legesse Negash, known for work related to tree propagation and forestry; Dr Tewolde Berhan Gebre Egziabher, known for biodiversity and biosafety work; and Professor Yalemtsehay Mekonnen, known for research in physiology and medicinal plants. Ethiopian research institutions include the Armauer Hansen Research Institute (AHRI), Ethiopian Public Health Institute (EPHI), Ethiopian Biodiversity Institute (EBI), and Ethiopian Institute of Agricultural Research (EIAR). Confirm current institutional names and the textbook's exact coverage against reliable sources.

sections.title: The Compound Light Microscope
sections.content: A compound light microscope uses lenses and visible light to magnify small specimens. Common parts include the eyepiece (ocular lens), objective lenses, stage, stage clips, light source or mirror, diaphragm, coarse-adjustment knob, fine-adjustment knob, arm, and base. Total magnification is calculated by multiplying eyepiece magnification by objective magnification. Use the coarse adjustment carefully, especially at high power, to avoid damaging the slide or lens. A 100× objective is commonly an oil-immersion objective and requires the appropriate procedure.

worked_examples.title: Calculating Total Magnification
worked_examples.problem: A microscope has a 10× eyepiece and a 40× objective. Find the total magnification. If an object is 0.015 mm long, what is its image length at this magnification?
worked_examples.solution: Total magnification = 10 × 40 = 400×. Image length = actual length × magnification = 0.015 mm × 400 = 6 mm.

activities.title: Observing Onion Epidermis
activities.procedure: With teacher supervision, prepare a thin onion epidermis slide, add a suitable drop of stain such as iodine if instructed, place a coverslip carefully, and observe under low power before moving to higher power. Use the fine-adjustment knob for clearer focus at higher magnification. Follow laboratory safety instructions and dispose of materials properly.

units.summary: Biology helps explain life and supports health, agriculture, and conservation. Microscopes make small structures visible, and total magnification is the product of eyepiece and objective magnifications.

practice_questions.question: Which Ethiopian scientist is associated with research on endod and freshwater snails involved in schistosomiasis transmission?
practice_questions.explanation: Dr Aklilu Lemma is known for research on endod and its potential molluscicidal use.

practice_questions.question: Which microscope adjustment is normally used for precise focusing at high power?
practice_questions.explanation: The fine-adjustment knob makes small focus changes and helps avoid striking the slide with the objective.

practice_questions.question: A 20 μm cell is viewed using a 15× eyepiece and a 40× objective. What is the image length?
practice_questions.explanation: Total magnification is 15 × 40 = 600×. Image length = 20 μm × 600 = 12,000 μm = 12 mm.

learning_objectives: Describe cell theory and distinguish prokaryotic from eukaryotic cells.
Identify major cell organelles and their functions.
Explain diffusion, osmosis, and active transport.

sections.title: Cell Theory and Cell Types
sections.content: Cell theory states that living organisms consist of one or more cells, the cell is the basic structural and functional unit of life, and new cells arise from existing cells. Prokaryotic cells lack a membrane-bound nucleus; eukaryotic cells have a nucleus and other membrane-bound organelles. Bacteria are prokaryotic, while animals, plants, fungi, and protists are eukaryotic.

sections.title: Organelles and Functions
sections.content: Key organelles include the nucleus (stores genetic material/DNA), mitochondria (site of most aerobic respiration and ATP generation), chloroplasts (site of photosynthesis in plants and some other organisms; contain chlorophyll), ribosomes (protein synthesis), endoplasmic reticulum (rough ER helps synthesize and process proteins; smooth ER synthesizes lipids), Golgi apparatus (modifies and packages materials), and cell membrane (selectively permeable barrier regulating transport). Plant cells also typically have a cellulose cell wall and a large central vacuole.

sections.title: Cell Transport Mechanisms
sections.content: Diffusion is the net movement of particles from a region of higher concentration to lower concentration down a concentration gradient; it does not directly require cellular energy. Osmosis is the net movement of water across a selectively permeable membrane from higher water potential (more dilute solution) toward lower water potential (more concentrated solution). Active transport moves substances against their concentration or electrochemical gradient using energy, often ATP, and membrane transport proteins.

worked_examples.title: Osmosis in Red Blood Cells
worked_examples.problem: Explain what happens to a red blood cell placed in (a) a hypertonic salt solution and (b) pure water.
worked_examples.solution: (a) In a hypertonic solution, water leaves the cell by osmosis, so it shrinks (crenation). (b) In a hypotonic solution such as pure water, water enters the cell; it swells and may burst (haemolysis) because it has no cell wall.

activities.title: Demonstrating Osmosis Using a Potato
activities.procedure: With teacher supervision, scoop a cavity in a peeled potato half, add concentrated sugar solution to the cavity, and place the potato in a container of water so the outside remains in contact with water. Observe changes in liquid level. Discuss how water moves across the potato tissue. Results may vary with potato size, solution concentration, and time.

units.summary: Cells are the basic units of life. Eukaryotic cells contain specialized organelles. Particles can move by diffusion, water can move by osmosis, and active transport uses energy to move substances against a gradient.

practice_questions.question: Which organelle is the main site of ATP production during aerobic respiration?
practice_questions.explanation: Mitochondria are the main site of ATP production during aerobic respiration in eukaryotic cells.

practice_questions.question: What happens to a plant cell placed in a strongly hypertonic solution?
options: It gains water and bursts immediately
It becomes a red blood cell
practice_questions.explanation: Water leaves the plant cell and the plasma membrane pulls away from the cell wall; this is plasmolysis.

practice_questions.question: Which transport process uses energy to move substances against a concentration gradient?
practice_questions.explanation: Active transport uses energy and transport proteins to move substances against a gradient.

learning_objectives: Identify essential nutrients and explain balanced diet requirements.
Explain digestion and nutrient absorption.
Describe respiration, circulation, and excretion.
Explain examples of communicable and non-communicable diseases and ways to reduce risk.

sections.title: Nutrition and Digestive System
sections.content: Nutrients include carbohydrates, proteins, lipids, vitamins, minerals, and water; dietary fibre supports healthy bowel function. Mechanical digestion physically breaks food into smaller pieces. Chemical digestion uses enzymes: salivary amylase begins starch digestion, pepsin digests proteins in the stomach, and lipases digest lipids into fatty acids and glycerol. Most digested nutrients are absorbed through villi and microvilli in the small intestine.

sections.title: Respiration and Gas Exchange
sections.content: Breathing moves air into and out of the lungs. In the alveoli, oxygen diffuses into surrounding capillaries and carbon dioxide diffuses from the blood into the alveoli. Cellular respiration releases energy from glucose; aerobic respiration uses oxygen and produces carbon dioxide, water, and usable energy transferred to ATP.

sections.title: Circulatory and Excretory Systems
sections.content: The human heart has four chambers: two atria and two ventricles. Pulmonary circulation carries blood between the heart and lungs; systemic circulation carries blood between the heart and the rest of the body. The kidneys filter blood and regulate water and salts. Nephrons form urine while useful substances are selectively reabsorbed.

sections.title: Disease Prevention and Health
sections.content: Communicable diseases are caused by infectious agents and can spread directly or indirectly; prevention can include vaccination where available, handwashing, safe water, sanitation, vector control, and appropriate medical care. Non-communicable diseases are not transmitted from person to person and may be associated with genetic, environmental, and lifestyle factors. Symptoms alone do not always identify a disease, so diagnosis and treatment should be handled by qualified health professionals.

worked_examples.title: Calculating an Average Reaction Rate
worked_examples.problem: If 10 g of starch is digested completely in 5 minutes, calculate the average rate of starch digestion.
worked_examples.solution: Average rate = mass digested ÷ time = 10 g ÷ 5 min = 2 g/min.

activities.title: Food Tests for Starch and Reducing Sugars
activities.procedure: With teacher supervision, add iodine solution to a food sample; a blue-black colour indicates starch. For reducing sugars, mix a sample with Benedict's solution and heat it in a hot-water bath, not directly over a flame. A colour change from blue toward green, yellow, orange, or brick-red can indicate increasing amounts of reducing sugar. Wear eye protection and follow laboratory instructions.

units.summary: Digestion enables nutrient absorption, respiration supports gas exchange and energy release, circulation transports substances, and excretion removes metabolic wastes. Good hygiene, prevention measures, and appropriate healthcare help reduce disease risks.

practice_questions.question: Which reagent turns blue-black when starch is present?
practice_questions.explanation: Iodine solution gives a blue-black colour in the presence of starch.

practice_questions.question: Where does most absorption of digested nutrients occur?
practice_questions.explanation: The villi and microvilli of the small intestine provide a large surface area for nutrient absorption.

practice_questions.question: Which heart chamber pumps deoxygenated blood into the pulmonary artery?
practice_questions.explanation: The right ventricle pumps deoxygenated blood toward the lungs through the pulmonary artery.

learning_objectives: Classify bacteria, viruses, fungi, and protozoa.
Explain useful industrial and ecological roles of microorganisms.
Describe the role of decomposers in nutrient cycling.
Explain examples of microbial diseases and their prevention.

sections.title: Types and Structure of Microorganisms
sections.content: Bacteria are unicellular prokaryotes; many have cell walls containing peptidoglycan and may be shaped as cocci, bacilli, or spirals. Viruses are acellular infectious agents containing DNA or RNA within a protein coat and can reproduce only inside host cells. Fungi such as yeasts and moulds are eukaryotes with chitin-containing cell walls. Protozoa are diverse unicellular eukaryotes; examples include Amoeba and Plasmodium, the parasite that causes malaria.

sections.title: Industrial and Ecological Roles
sections.content: Yeast such as Saccharomyces cerevisiae ferments sugars and releases carbon dioxide and ethanol; carbon dioxide helps dough rise. Microorganisms also contribute to food fermentation, decomposition, wastewater treatment, and nutrient cycling. Some Rhizobium bacteria live in legume root nodules and fix atmospheric nitrogen into ammonia/ammonium compounds that can enter the nitrogen cycle. Nitrogen fixation does not directly mean that the bacteria produce nitrate.

sections.title: Microorganisms and Disease
sections.content: Microorganisms differ in how they cause disease and spread. Malaria is caused by Plasmodium and is transmitted by infected female Anopheles mosquitoes. Tuberculosis is caused by bacteria in the Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex and usually spreads through the air from an infectious person. Prevention differs by disease and can include vector control, vaccination where appropriate, ventilation, testing, and treatment by health professionals.

worked_examples.title: Bacterial Binary Fission Growth
worked_examples.problem: A bacterial population doubles every 20 minutes. Starting with 100 bacteria, calculate the total after 2 hours, assuming ideal conditions and no deaths.
worked_examples.solution: 2 hours = 120 minutes. Number of generations = 120 ÷ 20 = 6. Population = 100 × 2⁶ = 100 × 64 = 6,400 bacteria.

activities.title: Observing Yeast Fermentation
activities.procedure: With adult or teacher supervision, mix warm (not hot) water, a little sugar, and baker's yeast in a clean bottle. Fit a balloon loosely over the opening and leave it in a warm place. Observe whether the balloon expands as gas is produced. Do not seal the mixture in a rigid airtight container.

units.summary: Microorganisms include bacteria, viruses, fungi, and protozoa. Some cause disease, while others support decomposition, nitrogen cycling, and food production. The correct prevention method depends on the organism and its route of transmission.

practice_questions.question: Which of the following is acellular and must use a host cell to replicate?
practice_questions.explanation: Viruses lack the cellular machinery needed for independent replication.

practice_questions.question: Which bacterial genus commonly forms nitrogen-fixing root nodules with legumes?
practice_questions.explanation: Rhizobium species can form symbiotic associations with legumes and fix atmospheric nitrogen.

practice_questions.question: A culture starts with 50 bacterial cells and doubles every 30 minutes. How many cells are present after 3 hours under ideal conditions?
practice_questions.explanation: Three hours is 180 minutes, giving six doublings: 50 × 2⁶ = 3,200 cells.

learning_objectives: Classify plants into non-vascular and vascular groups.
Explain leaf structure and photosynthesis.
Describe transpiration and transport through xylem and phloem.
Describe sexual reproduction in flowering plants.

sections.title: Plant Diversity and Anatomy
sections.content: Bryophytes such as mosses are non-vascular plants. Vascular plants include seedless groups such as ferns and seed plants, which include gymnosperms and angiosperms. Xylem transports water and mineral ions, mainly from roots toward leaves. Phloem transports sugars and other organic substances from sources, such as photosynthesizing leaves, to sinks such as roots, fruits, and growing tissues.

sections.title: Photosynthesis
sections.content: A simplified overall equation for photosynthesis is 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + light energy → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂. Light-dependent reactions occur in thylakoid membranes and produce ATP and NADPH while releasing oxygen from water. The Calvin cycle occurs in the chloroplast stroma and fixes carbon dioxide into small carbon compounds that can be used to make sugars; it does not directly produce glucose as its immediate product.

sections.title: Transpiration and Plant Reproduction
sections.content: Transpiration is the loss of water vapour, mainly through leaf stomata. It contributes to water movement through xylem. In flowering plants, stamens produce pollen and the carpel contains the stigma, style, and ovary. After pollination, a pollen tube may grow toward an ovule. In angiosperms, double fertilization produces a diploid zygote and usually triploid endosperm; the ovule develops into a seed and the ovary often develops into a fruit.

worked_examples.title: Calculating Water Uptake Rate
worked_examples.problem: In a potometer demonstration, a water bubble moves 50 mm along a capillary tube in 10 minutes. Calculate the average bubble movement rate.
worked_examples.solution: Average rate = distance ÷ time = 50 mm ÷ 10 min = 5 mm/min. A potometer estimates water uptake; it does not directly measure all water lost by transpiration.

activities.title: Flower Dissection
activities.procedure: With teacher supervision, examine a locally available flower such as Hibiscus. Identify sepals, petals, stamens (anther and filament), and carpel/pistil (stigma, style, and ovary). Avoid tasting plant parts and wash hands after handling specimens.

units.summary: Plants vary in vascular structure and reproduction. Xylem moves water and minerals, phloem transports organic nutrients, and photosynthesis stores light energy in chemical compounds. Flowering plants reproduce through pollination and fertilization.

practice_questions.question: Which tissue mainly transports water and dissolved mineral ions from roots toward leaves?
practice_questions.explanation: Xylem conducts water and mineral ions through the plant.

practice_questions.question: Where does the Calvin cycle occur in a chloroplast?
practice_questions.explanation: The Calvin cycle's carbon-fixation reactions occur in the chloroplast stroma.

practice_questions.question: In typical angiosperm double fertilization, which tissue is usually triploid?
practice_questions.explanation: One sperm nucleus fuses with two polar nuclei to form the usually triploid endosperm.

learning_objectives: Classify major invertebrate groups and vertebrates.
Compare symmetry and body cavity types.
Explain homeostasis and thermoregulation.
Recognize the ecological importance of Ethiopian wildlife.

sections.title: Animal Classification and Body Plans
sections.content: Major invertebrate groups include Porifera, Cnidaria, Platyhelminthes, Nematoda, Annelida, Mollusca, Echinodermata, and Arthropoda. Vertebrates are members of Chordata and include fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds, and mammals. Animals may have radial or bilateral symmetry. Common introductory body-cavity categories include acoelomate, pseudocoelomate, and coelomate.

sections.title: Thermoregulation and Homeostasis
sections.content: Homeostasis is the regulation of internal conditions within limits. Many reptiles and amphibians depend strongly on external heat sources and are described as ectothermic; birds and mammals generate much of their body heat metabolically and are endothermic. In humans, when body temperature rises, sweating and skin vasodilation increase heat loss. When cold, skin vasoconstriction and shivering help conserve or generate heat. Ectothermy/endothermy and poikilothermy/homeothermy are related but not identical terms.

sections.title: Ethiopian Wildlife and Conservation
sections.content: Ethiopia has distinctive wildlife and ecosystems. The Walia ibex (Capra walie) and Ethiopian wolf (Canis simensis) are endemic mammals associated with highland habitats. Wildlife supports biodiversity, ecological balance, tourism, and cultural value. Habitat loss, fragmentation, disease, and human-wildlife conflict can threaten species. Conservation may involve protected areas, habitat restoration, research, and community participation.

worked_examples.title: Negative Feedback in Thermoregulation
worked_examples.problem: Describe how the human body responds when its internal temperature rises above its normal range.
worked_examples.solution: Thermoreceptors and the hypothalamus detect the change. Signals increase sweating and cause skin blood vessels to dilate, promoting heat loss. As body temperature returns toward its normal range, the responses decrease through negative feedback.

activities.title: Comparing Arthropod Features
activities.procedure: Use pictures or safely observed specimens rather than handling unknown animals. Compare body regions and leg numbers: insects typically have three pairs of legs, arachnids four pairs, and myriapods many pairs. Record observations and return any safely observed living animals to their habitat.

units.summary: Animals show a wide range of body plans and adaptations. Homeostasis keeps internal conditions within suitable limits, and Ethiopian wildlife has ecological and economic importance that makes conservation valuable.

practice_questions.question: Which invertebrate group has jointed appendages and a chitinous exoskeleton?
practice_questions.explanation: Arthropods characteristically have jointed appendages and an exoskeleton.

practice_questions.question: Which response helps reduce heat loss from the skin in a cold environment?
practice_questions.explanation: Vasoconstriction reduces blood flow near the skin surface and helps limit heat loss.

practice_questions.question: The Walia ibex and Ethiopian wolf belong to which vertebrate class?
